newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Primakov says Russia still rejects NATO expansion.
newsitem.headline: Primakov says Russia still rejects NATO expansion.

text.p: Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov repeated on Wednesday that Moscow wants guarantees of its own security if NATO expands into eastern Europe and would take "retaliatory measures" against an enlarged Western bloc.

But he said, in contrast to recent comments from Kremlin security chief Alexander Lebed, that Russia saw no return to Cold War and recognised it was not in a position to prevent the Western defence alliance accepting former Soviet bloc members.

"In all the negotiations we have, our extremely negative attitude to NATO expansion is constant," Primakov said in an interview with NTV television. But he added: "We don't want to slide into a Cold War."

Lebed, an outspoken former general, said on Tuesday: "NATO's expansion eastwards will take us back to hostility and to the spirit of confrontation." He added: "We have missiles, which are rusty but still effective, as a deterrent argument."
Primakov said Lebed was entitled to his views but stressed President Boris Yeltsin had stipulated that the foreign ministry was in charge of foreign policy.
Primakov said Lebed was right to say Russia would take "counter-measures" if NATO did take in new members.
But he added: "We're not talking about firing rockets."
He noted that Defence Minister Igor Rodionov told NATO ministers in Norway last week that Russia would take unspecificied "retaliatory measures" if NATO expanded.
Primakov said these would concern "military structures" but declined to reveal what the measures might be.
He ruled out economic sanctions against Western businesses in Russia -- an idea raised in an interview by Lebed to a British newspaper last month. Lebed denied he made the remarks.
Primakov said Moscow could not rule out refusing to sign a projected charter with NATO if it failed to protect Russia's interests.
He said, however, that Russia's worries could be reduced, for example, by modifications in its treaty with the United States on conventional weapons, which are being negotiated.

Such "corrections" he said could reduce Moscow's concern at NATO expansion and help in developing dialogue, which could take the form of Russia's participation in certain NATO structures although not membership of the alliance.
